traits.sexual_system.note: APweb, Canellales page, Winteraceae (read 2026-10-16): Tasmannia (about 50 of about 105 species) is usually dioecious, while Drimys has perfect flowers and DELTA codes the rest as hermaphrodite; hermaphrodite is the slight majority, and dioecious is close to half, so 'often' rather than the proposed 'sometimes'.

traits.flower_symmetry.note: DELTA, Winteraceae (read 2026-10-16): flowers regular to somewhat irregular, the perianth unequal but never two-lipped; radial is the usual state (qualified rather than bare because of the 'somewhat irregular' state).

traits.note: Watson and Dallwitz, The Families of Flowering Plants (DELTA data, items edited May 2026), family Winteraceae: leaves alternate; leaves simple; margins entire; veins pinnate; stipules absent; plants hermaphrodite, monoecious or polygamous; ovary superior; floral cup absent; stems woody; flowers solitary or in cymes; flowers actinomorphic or zygomorphic; perianth sepals and petals; fruit capsule, berry, follicle or aggregate; stamens 15 to 100; carpels (1-) 3 to 20. Read from the coded states by script (spec-rework/b1/delta/mapdelta.py); a state the authors qualify (rarely, usually, a share) keeps its word, an unqualified one beside a usual state reads as sometimes.

traits.zygomorphy.note: Watson and Dallwitz, The Families of Flowering Plants (DELTA data), family Winteraceae: its irregular flowers are of no named kind (pea flower, two lips, orchid lip), read from the coded corolla symmetry (spec-rework/b1/delta): zygomorphy other. Its flowers are not mostly zygomorphic, so a plant of it states its own symmetry; one that is zygomorphic draws this kind, and one stating none is drawn regular.

traits.phyllotaxis_pattern.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 200, 202, 203, family Winteraceae: phyllotaxis pattern spiral; read as "spiral".

traits.leaf_habit.note: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 200, 202, 203, family Winteraceae: leaf habit evergreen; read as "evergreen".

traits.stamens.note: Rare extremes noted only; the count's source is the family's `traits` note. The books give the family low 3: Simpson, Plant Systematics (2019) p. 200, 202, 203: 3-∞. Left out of the range on the owner's go (2026-10-15): they belong to some of its genera, and a family's rare ends would reach every species that inherits its count.
